concept.name: Adversarial test
concept.definition: Deliberately probing an AI system with inputs designed to make it fail — evasion attacks, poisoned data, prompt injections, extraction attempts — in order to find vulnerabilities before an adversary does. NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy (NIST AI 100-2) classifies such attacks by ML method, lifecycle stage, and attacker goals, capabilities, and knowledge, and pairs them with mitigations.
concept.intuition: Hire the burglar to test the locks: instead of asking 'does it work?', ask 'how can it be made to break?'
concept.mechanics: Testers enumerate the attack surface (inputs, retrieved content, tools, training data) and mount attack classes from the taxonomy — e.g., crafting inputs that bypass safety controls or manipulate decisions — then record success rates and trace them to mitigations such as input filtering, least privilege, and human approval for high-risk actions. Penetration-testing practice treats the model as an untrusted user.
concept.failure_modes: A passed adversarial test proves only that the tested attacks failed — novel attack classes and adaptive attackers evolve past any fixed test suite. Tests scoped to the model alone miss system-level paths (tools, retrieval corpora, downstream consumers of output).
concept.misconceptions: Adversarial testing is not the same as accuracy testing on hard examples; it assumes an intelligent opponent who adapts. Red teaming once, pre-launch, is not a durable defense — it must recur as the system and attack landscape change.
concept.example: Before enabling a trading assistant's report-summarization feature, testers feed it research PDFs containing hidden injected instructions and verify that approval gates and output filters block every attempted policy override.

citations.source: NIST AI 100-2 E2025, 'Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations'
